q: A compound C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown. Which structure fits?
h: Find the C=O band position first (conjugated or not), then ask whether there is an aldehyde H near δ 9–10.
w: DBE = 5: a benzene ring (4) plus one C=O. The strong band at 1685 cm−1 is a C=O lowered about 30 cm−1 by conjugation with the ring, and there is no aldehyde C–H pair near 2720/2820 cm−1 and no signal at δ 9–10. The aromatic pattern 2H : 1H : 2H (d, t, t) with 5H total is a monosubstituted ring, and the 3H singlet at δ 2.60 is a CH3 on a C=O. The compound is acetophenone.
x: Phenylacetaldehyde has an unconjugated CHO: C=O near 1725 cm<sup>−1</sup>, a 1H triplet near δ 9.7 and a 2H doublet near δ 3.6, none of which appear.
4-Methylbenzaldehyde has a 1H singlet near δ 9.9 (CHO), the C–H pair at 2720/2820 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and only 4 aromatic H as two 2H doublets.
2-Methylbenzaldehyde shows a CHO singlet near δ 10.2 and four separate 1H aromatic signals, not a 2:1:2 pattern for 5H.

q: A compound C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub> gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown (the δ 12.0 signal disappears on shaking with D<sub>2</sub>O). Which structure fits?
h: A very broad band from about 3300 down to 2500 cm<sup>−1</sup> plus a 1H signal near δ 12 points to one functional group. Then read the aromatic pattern.
w: The very broad O–H band (3300–2500 cm−1) and the exchangeable 1H at δ 12.0 identify a carboxylic acid; the C=O at 1685 cm−1 is low because the COOH is conjugated with the ring. Two 2H doublets (δ 7.99 and 7.27) are the classic para-disubstituted pattern, and the 3H singlet at δ 2.43 is an aryl CH3. The compound is 4-methylbenzoic acid.
x: Methyl benzoate has no O–H (no broad band, no δ 12 signal); its CH<sub>3</sub> is an O–CH<sub>3</sub> singlet near δ 3.9, and its ring is monosubstituted (5H).
Phenylacetic acid has 5 aromatic H and a CH<sub>2</sub> singlet near δ 3.6; its COOH is not conjugated, so its C=O is near 1710 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
3-Methylbenzoic acid is meta-substituted: four different aromatic H (four 1H signals), not two 2H doublets.

q: A compound C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub> shows a strong IR band at 1740 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a strong band at 1230 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and the <sup>1</sup>H and <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectra shown. Which structure fits?
h: Where would a CH<sub>2</sub> appear if it were bonded to both an oxygen and a benzene ring? Where would CH<sub>3</sub> appear on O versus on C=O?
w: 1740 cm−1 with a strong C–O band at 1230 cm−1 is an unconjugated ester (13C 170.9). The 5H multiplet is a monosubstituted ring. The 2H singlet at δ 5.11 is far downfield because the CH2 is both benzylic and bonded to the ester O (13C 66.3), and the 3H singlet at δ 2.10 is a CH3–C=O (13C 21.0). This is benzyl acetate, PhCH2OC(=O)CH3.
x: Methyl phenylacetate also gives two singlets, but at δ 3.70 (OCH<sub>3</sub>, 13C ≈ 52) and δ 3.63 (ArCH<sub>2</sub>C=O, 13C ≈ 41); nothing would reach δ 5.1 or 66 ppm.
Ethyl benzoate shows an OCH<sub>2</sub> quartet (δ 4.38) and a CH<sub>3</sub> triplet (δ 1.38), and its conjugated ester C=O absorbs near 1720 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
4-Methoxyacetophenone is para-disubstituted (two 2H doublets, 4 ArH) and its conjugated ketone C=O is near 1675 cm<sup>−1</sup> with 13C near 197 ppm.

q: A compound has molecular formula C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>7</sub>ClO. Which set of structural features matches its degree of unsaturation?
c: A benzene ring and one C=O
A benzene ring and one C≡C
A benzene ring, one C=O and one more ring
h: DBE = (2C + 2 + N − H − X)/2. A halogen counts like a hydrogen.
w: DBE = (2·8 + 2 − 7 − 1)/2 = 10/2 = 5. A benzene ring accounts for 4 (one ring + three C=C), leaving one more: a benzene ring and one C=O (for example 4-chloroacetophenone).
x: A benzene ring alone is DBE 4; this formula has DBE 5, so one π bond or ring is missing.
A C≡C counts as 2, giving DBE 6, one too many.
Ring + C=O + benzene is DBE 6, one too many; the extra ring is not allowed.

q: A compound gives the mass spectrum and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown. Which structure fits?
h: Two molecular-ion peaks 2 units apart in a 1 : 1 ratio identify one halogen. Then count aromatic signals.
w: M+ at m/z 170 and 172 in about a 1 : 1 ratio means one Br (79Br and 81Br are nearly equally abundant); 170 − 79 = 91, the C7H7+ base peak. The two 2H doublets are a para-disubstituted ring and the 3H singlet at δ 2.30 is an aryl CH3: 4-bromotoluene.
x: Benzyl bromide has 5 aromatic H and a 2H CH<sub>2</sub>Br singlet near δ 4.5, not a 3H singlet at δ 2.30.
2-Bromotoluene is ortho-disubstituted: four different aromatic H, not two 2H doublets.
4-Chlorotoluene has M<sup>+</sup> at m/z 126 and 128 in a 3 : 1 ratio, not 170/172 at 1 : 1.

q: A compound shows a strong IR band at 1685 cm<sup>−1</sup> and gives the mass spectrum and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown. Which structure fits?
h: Check the M : M+2 ratio for the halogen, then the aromatic pattern, then where the CH<sub>3</sub> or CH<sub>2</sub> sits.
w: M+ 154 and M+2 156 in a 3 : 1 ratio means one Cl. The base peak at 139/141 is loss of CH3 (α-cleavage) to give ClC6H4CO+, still carrying Cl. Two 2H doublets mean para substitution, the 3H singlet at δ 2.59 is CH3C=O, and 1685 cm−1 is an aryl ketone: 4-chloroacetophenone.
x: 2-Chloro-1-phenylethanone has 5 aromatic H and a 2H singlet near δ 4.7 for CH<sub>2</sub>Cl; there is no 3H singlet.
4-Bromoacetophenone would give M<sup>+</sup> at 198/200 in a 1 : 1 ratio.
3-Chloroacetophenone is meta-substituted: four different 1H aromatic signals, not two 2H doublets.

q: The most downfield <sup>13</sup>C signal of a compound is at δ 207.5, and it is absent from both the DEPT-90 and DEPT-135 spectra. Which compound is it?
h: Match 13C carbonyl regions: ketone ≈ 205–210, aldehyde ≈ 200, ester/acid ≈ 170–180, nitrile ≈ 118–122. Then use DEPT: which carbons have no H?
w: δ 207.5 is in the ketone window, and a signal missing from DEPT-90 and DEPT-135 belongs to a carbon with no H (quaternary). A ketone C=O has no H; an aldehyde C=O is a CH and would appear in DEPT-90. So the compound is 4-phenylbutan-2-one.
x: 3-Phenylpropanal's CHO carbon is near δ 201 and is a CH, so it would appear (positive) in both DEPT-90 and DEPT-135.
An ester C=O such as that of methyl 3-phenylpropanoate is near δ 173, well upfield of 207.
A nitrile carbon is near δ 119; 3-phenylpropanenitrile has no signal anywhere near 207 ppm.

q: A compound C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>7</sub>N gives the IR, <sup>1</sup>H and <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectra shown. Which structure fits?
h: What absorbs sharply near 2230 cm<sup>−1</sup> with nothing near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>? Then read the aromatic pattern.
w: DBE = (16 + 2 + 1 − 7)/2 = 6: a benzene ring plus two more, fitting a C≡N. The sharp 2228 cm−1 band (low for a nitrile because it is conjugated with the ring) and the 13C signal at δ 119.1 confirm a nitrile; nothing appears near 3300 cm−1, so there is no N–H or ≡C–H. Two 2H doublets mean para substitution, and the 3H singlet at δ 2.42 is an aryl CH3: 4-methylbenzonitrile. (The 13C at δ 109.3 is the ring carbon bearing CN.)
x: Phenylacetonitrile has 5 aromatic H and a 2H CH<sub>2</sub> singlet near δ 3.7; its unconjugated C≡N absorbs near 2250 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
4-Ethynylaniline would show two N–H stretches (3300–3450 cm<sup>−1</sup>), a sharp ≡C–H stretch near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a ≡C–H singlet near δ 3.0.
Indole has an N–H stretch near 3400 cm<sup>−1</sup>, no triple-bond band, and six different aromatic/heteroaromatic C–H signals.

q: Isomers I and II (both C8H8O2) are shown. Which observation distinguishes them?
c: The CH<sub>3</sub> singlet: near δ 3.9 in I but near δ 2.3 in II
The molecular ion: m/z 136 for I but m/z 150 for II
The <sup>13</sup>C signal count: 6 for I but 5 for II
The aromatic integration: 5H for I but 4H for II
h: Both are esters with a monosubstituted ring and one CH<sub>3</sub>. What is the CH<sub>3</sub> bonded to in each?
w: In methyl benzoate (I) the CH3 is on the ester oxygen (O–CH3, δ ≈ 3.9). In phenyl acetate (II) the CH3 is on the carbonyl carbon (CH3–C=O, δ ≈ 2.3). So the CH3 singlet position tells them apart. (Their IR also differs: about 1725 cm−1 for I, conjugated with the ring, and about 1765 cm−1 for the aryl ester II.)
x: They are isomers with the same formula, so both have M<sup>+</sup> = 136.
Both have 6 carbon signals: C=O, CH<sub>3</sub>, and four ring signals (ipso, ortho, meta, para).
Both rings are monosubstituted, so both show 5 aromatic H.

q: Which 1H NMR data (CDCl3) belong to the major product of this reaction?
h: OCH<sub>3</sub> is an o/p director, and the bulky acylium ion prefers the less hindered position. What is added: an acetyl or a methyl?
w: Friedel–Crafts acylation puts an acetyl group on the ring. OCH3 directs ortho/para, and para wins on sterics, giving 4-methoxyacetophenone. Its spectrum: two 2H doublets (para), OCH3 at δ 3.87 and the acetyl CH3 at δ 2.55, deshielded by the C=O: δ 7.93 (d, 2H), 6.93 (d, 2H), 3.87 (s, 3H), 2.55 (s, 3H). The doublet at 7.93 is ortho to the electron-withdrawing C=O; the one at 6.93 is ortho to the donating OCH3.
x: Four separate 1H aromatic signals with ortho couplings fit the ortho product (2-methoxyacetophenone), which is the minor isomer.
Four aromatic H with a 1H triplet and a dd fit the meta product (3-methoxyacetophenone), which an o/p director like OCH<sub>3</sub> barely forms.
A CH<sub>3</sub> at δ 2.29 is an aryl methyl, as in 4-methylanisole. Acylation adds CH<sub>3</sub>C=O, whose CH<sub>3</sub> appears near δ 2.5–2.6.

q: Acetophenone is treated with NaBH<sub>4</sub> in CH<sub>3</sub>OH. Which spectral change shows that the reaction worked?
c: The 1685 cm<sup>−1</sup> band disappears and a broad 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup> band appears; the δ 2.60 CH<sub>3</sub> singlet becomes a doublet near δ 1.5, coupled to a new 1H quartet near δ 4.9
The C=O band moves from 1685 to about 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup> because conjugation with the ring is lost; the δ 2.60 CH<sub>3</sub> singlet is unchanged
The δ 2.60 CH<sub>3</sub> singlet moves to δ 1.5 and stays a singlet, and a new 1H singlet appears near δ 4.9
A very broad band from 3300 to 2500 cm<sup>−1</sup> appears, and a new exchangeable 1H singlet appears near δ 12
h: NaBH<sub>4</sub> reduces a ketone to a secondary alcohol. What is the new carbon bonded to, and what does the CH<sub>3</sub> now neighbor?
w: NaBH4 gives 1-phenylethanol, PhCH(OH)CH3. The C=O band is gone and an O–H band appears near 3350 cm−1. The CH3 now sits next to a CH (n + 1 = 2, a doublet near δ 1.5), and that CH (next to 3 H, a quartet) is at δ 4.9 because it carries O and Ph. So the C=O is replaced by O–H, and the CH3 singlet becomes a doublet coupled to a new 1H quartet.
x: The product has no C=O at all, so no C=O band remains to shift.
The CH<sub>3</sub> is now on a carbon that carries one H, so it is split into a doublet, and that CH is a quartet, not a singlet.
A 2500–3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> O–H and a δ 12 H describe a carboxylic acid; NaBH<sub>4</sub> reduces, it does not oxidize.

q: Which compound has the longest-wavelength UV absorption maximum (λ<sub>max</sub>)?
h: Count the C=C bonds that are in one continuous conjugated system (a benzene ring counts).
w: λmax increases as the conjugated π system grows, because the HOMO–LUMO gap shrinks. (E)-1-Phenyl-1,3-butadiene has a diene conjugated with a benzene ring (λmax ≈ 280 nm), the largest conjugated system here.
x: 1,3-Cyclohexadiene is a conjugated diene held s-cis (λ<sub>max</sub> ≈ 256 nm), but it has only two C=C in conjugation.
(2E,4E)-2,4-Hexadiene is a conjugated diene (λ<sub>max</sub> ≈ 227 nm); its methyl groups add only a few nm.
1,4-Cyclohexadiene's C=C bonds are separated by CH<sub>2</sub> groups, so they are not conjugated; it absorbs below 200 nm.

q: A compound C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>11</sub>N shows two medium IR bands at 3370 and 3290 cm<sup>−1</sup> and the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown (the δ 1.15 signal exchanges with D<sub>2</sub>O). Which structure fits?
h: Two N–H bands mean NH<sub>2</sub>. Then look at the aromatic integration and the coupling of the CH<sub>2</sub> groups.
w: Two N–H stretches (symmetric and asymmetric) mean a primary amine, and the 2H exchangeable signal at δ 1.15 is the NH2 of an alkylamine. The 5H multiplet is a monosubstituted ring, and two 2H triplets mean –CH2CH2–: δ 2.97 (CH2N) and 2.75 (ArCH2). The compound is 2-phenylethylamine.
x: N-Methylbenzylamine is a secondary amine with one N–H band, and it gives two singlets (CH<sub>2</sub> near δ 3.75, NCH<sub>3</sub> near δ 2.45), not two triplets.
N,N-Dimethylaniline is tertiary: no N–H band at all, and a 6H singlet near δ 2.9.
4-Ethylaniline is para-disubstituted (two 2H doublets) with an ArNH<sub>2</sub> near δ 3.5 and an ethyl quartet/triplet, not two triplets.

q: A compound C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>11</sub>NO gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown (the δ 7.20 signal exchanges with D<sub>2</sub>O). Which structure fits?
h: How many N–H bands, and where is the C=O? Then decide which CH<sub>3</sub> is on the ring and which is on the carbonyl.
w: DBE = 5: a ring plus one C=O. One N–H stretch (3290 cm−1) and a C=O at 1660 cm−1 with an amide II band at 1540 cm−1 mean a secondary amide (one N–H, 1H broad at δ 7.20). Two 2H doublets mean para substitution. The two 3H singlets are an aryl CH3 (δ 2.31) and an acetyl CH3 (δ 2.16). The compound is N-(4-methylphenyl)acetamide.
x: N,N-Dimethylbenzamide has no N–H (no band near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>), and its ring is monosubstituted (5H). Its two N–CH<sub>3</sub> singlets appear near δ 3.0 because of slow C–N rotation.
2-(4-Methylphenyl)acetamide is a primary amide: two N–H bands, a 2H NH<sub>2</sub>, and a 2H CH<sub>2</sub> singlet near δ 3.5 instead of a second 3H singlet.
4′-Aminopropiophenone has an NH<sub>2</sub> (two N–H bands) and an ethyl group (quartet near δ 2.9, triplet near δ 1.2), not two singlets.

q: A compound C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O<sub>3</sub> shows strong IR bands at 1825 and 1755 cm<sup>−1</sup> (none above 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup>) and the <sup>1</sup>H and <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectra shown. Which structure fits?
h: Which carbonyl derivative shows two C=O stretches, one above 1800 cm−1?
w: Two strong C=O bands about 60–70 cm−1 apart, the higher one above 1800 cm−1, are the symmetric and asymmetric stretches of an anhydride. One 6H singlet and only two 13C signals (C=O at δ 166.6, CH3 at δ 22.1) mean a symmetric molecule: acetic anhydride.
x: Methyl pyruvate has two different CH<sub>3</sub> groups (OCH<sub>3</sub> near δ 3.9, CH<sub>3</sub>C=O near δ 2.5) and a ketone 13C near δ 192; its C=O bands are near 1735–1750 cm<sup>−1</sup>, not 1825.
Acetoacetic acid has a carboxylic O–H (broad 2500–3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>), a CH<sub>2</sub> singlet, and a ketone 13C near δ 200.
(2-Oxopropyl) formate has a formyl H singlet near δ 8.1 and a CH<sub>2</sub> singlet near δ 4.7 in addition to a CH<sub>3</sub>; three signals, not one.

q: A compound C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown. Which structure fits?
h: A 1H singlet near δ 10 and weak IR bands near 2820 and 2730 cm<sup>−1</sup> point to one group. Then read the ring pattern and the alkyl signals.
w: The 1H singlet at δ 9.97 and the C–H pair at 2820/2730 cm−1 identify an aldehyde; the C=O at 1700 cm−1 is conjugated with the ring. It is a singlet, so the CHO is on the ring (no neighboring H). Two 2H doublets mean para substitution, and the quartet/triplet (δ 2.72, 1.27) is an aryl ethyl group: 4-ethylbenzaldehyde.
x: Propiophenone is a ketone: no δ 9.97 signal, no 2720 cm<sup>−1</sup> band, and a 5H monosubstituted ring.
3-Phenylpropanal's CHO is a triplet near δ 9.8 (coupled to CH<sub>2</sub>), with two CH<sub>2</sub> signals and a 5H ring.
2,4-Dimethylbenzaldehyde would show two separate 3H singlets near δ 2.4–2.6 and three different aromatic H, not an ethyl quartet and triplet.

q: A compound C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O shows a strong IR band at 1686 cm<sup>−1</sup>, a <sup>13</sup>C signal at δ 200.4, and the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown. Which structure fits?
h: Is the C=O conjugated with the ring? Then use the splitting of the alkyl signals to build the chain.
w: 1686 cm−1 and δ 200.4 fit an aryl ketone (conjugation lowers the C=O stretch from about 1715 and moves the 13C a little upfield of 207). The 2:1:2 aromatic pattern is a monosubstituted benzoyl group. The alkyl chain is t (2H, δ 2.95, next to C=O) – sextet (2H) – t (3H): CH2CH2CH3. The compound is 1-phenylbutan-1-one (butyrophenone).
x: 1-Phenylbutan-2-one has a CH<sub>2</sub> between ring and C=O that is a singlet near δ 3.7, plus an ethyl q/t; its C=O is unconjugated (≈1715 cm<sup>−1</sup>, δ ≈ 209).
4-Phenylbutan-2-one shows a CH<sub>3</sub>C=O singlet near δ 2.1 and two triplets; its C=O is unconjugated (≈1715 cm<sup>−1</sup>, δ ≈ 208).
2-Methyl-1-phenylpropan-1-one is also an aryl ketone, but its isopropyl group gives a 1H septet near δ 3.5 and a 6H doublet near δ 1.2.

q: A compound C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>2</sub> shows a strong IR band at 1716 cm<sup>−1</sup> and strong bands at 1275 and 1105 cm<sup>−1</sup>. Its <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum is shown. Which structure fits?
h: An ethyl quartet near δ 4.3 and one near δ 2.5 mean different things. Which side of the ester O is the ethyl on?
w: The C=O at 1716 cm−1 with strong C–O bands is a conjugated (aryl) ester. The ethyl CH2 quartet at δ 4.36 must be on oxygen (O–CH2); a CH2–C=O would be near δ 2.5. Two 2H doublets, with the δ 7.94 pair ortho to the C=O, mean para substitution, and δ 2.40 is an aryl CH3. The compound is ethyl 4-methylbenzoate.
x: In 4-methylphenyl propanoate the ethyl is on the acyl side: its CH<sub>2</sub> quartet is near δ 2.6, and an aryl ester C=O absorbs near 1760 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
Propyl benzoate has a 5H monosubstituted ring and an OCH<sub>2</sub> triplet, a sextet and a CH<sub>3</sub> triplet; there is no aryl CH<sub>3</sub> singlet.
Ethyl phenylacetate has a 5H ring, a CH<sub>2</sub> singlet near δ 3.6 and an OCH<sub>2</sub> quartet near δ 4.15; its unconjugated C=O is near 1740 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

q: A compound C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub> gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown (the δ 11.5 signal exchanges with D<sub>2</sub>O). Which structure fits?
h: Identify the functional group from the O–H shape and the δ 11.5 proton. Is the C=O conjugated? Then read the splitting of the CH<sub>2</sub> groups.
w: The broad 3300–2500 cm−1 O–H and the exchangeable δ 11.5 H mean a carboxylic acid. Its C=O at 1710 cm−1 is not lowered, so the COOH is not on the ring. A 5H multiplet (monosubstituted ring) and two 2H triplets (ArCH2CH2COOH) give 3-phenylpropanoic acid.
x: 4-Ethylbenzoic acid has a para pattern (two 2H doublets), an ethyl quartet/triplet, and a conjugated C=O near 1685 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
2-Phenylpropanoic acid shows a 1H quartet near δ 3.7 and a 3H doublet near δ 1.5, not two 2H triplets.
Methyl phenylacetate is an ester: no O–H band and no δ 11.5 signal, and it shows two singlets (OCH<sub>3</sub> and CH<sub>2</sub>).

q: An aromatic hydrocarbon C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>10</sub> shows <sup>1</sup>H NMR δ 7.12 (m, 4H), 2.27 (s, 6H) and the <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum shown. Which structure fits?
h: The 1H spectrum fits more than one isomer. Count unique carbons in each using its symmetry.
w: A 6H singlet means two equivalent aryl CH3 groups, so the compound is a xylene, and the 13C spectrum decides which one. o-Xylene has a mirror plane through the ring between the two CH3 groups: 2 ring C bearing CH3, 2 pairs of ring CH, and 1 CH3 type = 4 signals (δ 136.5, 129.6, 125.8, 19.7). The answer is 1,2-dimethylbenzene.
x: m-Xylene has 5 carbon signals: C1/C3, C2, C4/C6, C5 and CH<sub>3</sub>.
p-Xylene has only 3 carbon signals, and its 4 ring H are equivalent (a sharp singlet).
Ethylbenzene shows an ethyl quartet/triplet in the 1H spectrum, not a 6H singlet, and 6 carbon signals.
